title: Research Bite #17: Learning Styles: Concepts and Evidence
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #17 covers Pashler, McDaniel, Rohrer, and Bjork's widely-cited review "Learning Styles: Concepts and Evidence," which set out to test whether tailoring instruction to a student's preferred learning style (visual, auditory, kinesthetic, etc.) actually improves outcomes. The authors searched for studies using the only research design that could validly test the claim -- one that classifies learners by style, then randomly assigns each to instruction matched or mismatched to that style, and looks for a genuine interaction effect -- and found almost none met that bar. The handful of adequately designed studies mostly failed to find the predicted interaction, leading the authors to conclude there is no adequate evidence base for using learning-style assessments to guide instruction. They stop short of denying that people differ in ability and preference, but argue those differences don't translate into a validated case for style-matched teaching. Barton's takeaway for teachers is to redirect the money and time currently spent on learning-styles inventories toward practices with a real evidence base, such as retrieval practice, while remaining open to future research on genuine aptitude-by-treatment interactions.
points: The review's core methodological point: only a classify-then-randomly-assign design can test whether learning styles matter, and studies using that design overwhelmingly failed to find the predicted interaction.

Aptitude-by-treatment interactions do exist in some contexts (e.g., more structured instruction favoring lower-ability learners), but they don't map onto the visual/auditory/kinesthetic categories peddled by commercial learning-styles assessments.
The authors' warning that people hold beliefs about how they learn that are "faulty," which can lead both teachers and students toward self-defeating study and teaching choices.
The practical redirect: resources spent on learning-styles diagnostics would be better spent on instructional approaches with a demonstrated evidence base.
quotes: This article examines the concept of “learning styles,” the idea that individuals learn best through methods tailored to their preferences. The authors investigated whether scientific evidence supports the widespread use of learning-styles assessments in education.

Their review of existing literature revealed a lack of robust evidence validating the practice of tailoring instruction to assessed learning styles. They argue that properly designed experiments, demonstrating a specific interaction between learning style and instructional method, are critically missing.
At present, there is no adequate evidence base to justify incorporating learning-styles assessments into general educational practice

A few studies are consistent with the idea that structured instruction produces better learning outcomes for students of lower ability (relative to less structured instruction), whereas less structured instruction produces better learning outcomes for students with higher abilities (relative to structured instruction).

There is growing evidence that people hold beliefs about how they learn that are faulty in various ways, which frequently lead people to manage their own learning and teach others in non-optimal ways.
The finding that learners’ memory for information or procedures can be directly enhanced through testing is not something that applies to only a small subset of learners but applies to all.
